newsitem.title: UK: Clone scientists seek to dispel fear over Dolly.
newsitem.headline: Clone scientists seek to dispel fear over Dolly.

text.p: Dolly is woolly and alert, with a soft pink nose and an appealing air that scientists hope will help dispel fears about the fact that she is a clone.
The sheep at the heart of an international furore over the first-ever successful cloning of an adult animal was introduced to the world on Tuesday, along with her creators.
They were at pains to stress that they hope Dolly and her kind can benefit humanity, and quick to denounce any talk of cloning humans or any other type of "Frankenstein" science.
The creation of Dolly sparked fears that it could only be a short step from cloning sheep to doing the same to humans.
Ian Wilmut, who headed the team that created Dolly from a ewe's egg cell and a mammary gland cell taken from a second ewe, denied he had taken science to the brink of cloning humans.
"We have made it clear -- we can't see a clinical reason why you would do it," Wilmut told reporters invited to visit the Roslin Institute near Edinburgh where the work was done.

Ron James, Managing Director of PPL Pharmaceuticals, which sponsored and is patenting the work, agreed. "In big capital letters, it (cloning humans) is not immediately possible," he said. "And I hope it never happens."

News of Wilmut's discovery, to be published this week in the scientific journal Nature, prompted fearful speculation about what unethical scientists might do with the knowledge. Trying to clone humans is illegal in Britain but not elsewhere.

On Monday night U.S. President Bill Clinton reacted to the news about Dolly by asking an expert panel to review the legal and ethical ramifications of cloning with special regard to any implications for humans.
Clinton signed an executive order in 1995 banning government funding for the creation of human embryos.

Wilmut welcomed Clinton's move. "We see it as our job to inform," he said, stressing that British watchdogs such as the Nuffield Council on Bioethics, a panel of scientists and other experts, and the goverment-appointed Human Fertilisation and Embryology Authority, had been fully briefed on the work.
"We would entirely welcome the passing of laws in the U.S. which would prevent human cloning," James added.

The PPL and Roslin scientists are acutely aware of the controversy surrounding genetic manipulation and testing. They currently work together to genetically engineer sheep that produce milk with human proteins that are in clinical trials for use in treating cystic fibrosis, a chronic and debilitating genetic disease.

Last year street demonstrations broke out in several European cities over the news that genetically engineered soybeans from the United States would be used, unlabelled, in products ranging from bread to ice cream.
But Alan Colman, research director for PPL, said his company was producing medicine, not food, and people saw this differently.
"I think it is undoubtedly true that when dealing with life or death issues, things become more acceptable," he said.
"There are no projects in progress (here) to modify animals in a way that would be associated with food," Wilmut added.
PPL was prepared for controversy and, ahead of publication in Nature, they hired a team of public relations experts to explain their work.

"I think it was entirely predictable that there would be people out there saying silly things like can you clone a dinosaur," James said. "It's obvious that this is something that people are going to want to discuss."

And Dolly offers perhaps the best testimony. An obviously healthy sheep, she nuzzled outstretched hands and bounced confidently around her straw-filled pen in a corrugated metal barn on the institute's grounds.

Asked how she got her name, Wilmut noted that she sprang from the fusion of a mammary gland cell. "No one could think of a more impressive set of mammary glands than (country and western singer) Dolly Parton."
